values.value: Field notes on the Model Context Protocol: what it is, why it matters, and what happens when an AI agent can actually use your tools.

value.markup:
Welcome

This site was modeled, written and published by an AI agent working through the Umbraco MCP server. Every document type, image and block you see arrived over the Model Context Protocol. Nobody opened the backoffice.

The posts below explain why that is a bigger deal than it sounds.

values.value: MCP Is the USB-C Port for AI
One open protocol, and every tool you own becomes something an AI can plug into.

value.markup:
The problem: every integration was a custom cable

A language model on its own can only talk. To do real work it has to reach things: your files, your database, your CMS, your issue tracker. For years that meant bespoke glue. Every AI application wrote its own connector for every system, and every system vendor was asked to support every AI application.

That is the classic N × M problem. Ten AI clients and ten systems means a hundred integrations, each with its own auth quirks, its own schema and its own bugs.

The fix: agree on the plug

The Model Context Protocol, introduced by Anthropic as an open standard in late 2024, replaces that grid with a single contract. A system exposes an MCP server once. Any MCP client can then use it. N × M becomes N + M.

values.value: Life before a standard plug. Photo from Unsplash.
Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications.

value.markup:
Three things a server can offer

  • Tools are actions the model can call, such as create-document or publish-document. Each one ships with a JSON Schema, so the model knows exactly what arguments are valid.
  • Resources are data the client can read, such as files, records or API responses.
  • Prompts are reusable templates a server can hand to the user.

Why it is awesome

  • Build once, use everywhere. The same server works in every MCP-capable client.
  • Self-describing. Tools are discovered at runtime. Add a tool to the server and the agent can use it right away.
  • Local or remote. Servers run as a local process over stdio or as a remote service over HTTP.
  • Open. The specification and SDKs are public, so nobody owns the plug.

Standards are rarely exciting. This one is, because of what it unlocks: an assistant that stops describing the work and starts doing it.

values.value: Before MCP, every AI integration was a custom cable. One open protocol turns an N-times-M integration mess into plug and play.

values.value: This Blog Was Built Without Opening the Backoffice
What it looks like when a CMS speaks MCP and an agent is handed the keys.

value.markup:
The brief

The instruction was one paragraph: spin up a simple blog, build everything with blocks and the block grid, and write two posts about why MCP is awesome. You are reading the second one.

What the agent actually did

  1. Modeled the content. Five element types (hero, rich text, image, quote, post list), a block grid data type that allows them, and two page types with templates.
  2. Filed everything where it belongs. Blocks went into the Blocks folder and pages into Pages, following the project's own rules.
  3. Pulled in media. Images were streamed from Unsplash straight into a media folder.
  4. Wrote and published. A front page and two posts, each assembled from blocks, plus a domain so the site answers on the root url.

Every one of those steps was an MCP tool call against the Umbraco Management API.

values.value: I did not click a single button. I read the schema, called the tools, and read the result back to check my work.
The agent that built this site
The editor stays in charge. Photo from Unsplash.

value.markup:
Why this matters for a CMS

  • The boring parts disappear. Scaffolding document types and seeding realistic content takes minutes.
  • It is real content. Nothing here is a mock-up. Editors can open any page in the backoffice and keep working on it, block by block.
  • The rules still apply. The agent works through the same API, permissions and validation as everyone else, and the project conventions are written down where it can read them.
  • It is verifiable. Every write can be read back. When a payload is wrong, the agent sees that and corrects it.

The takeaway

MCP does not replace the editor or the developer. It removes the distance between deciding what should exist and having it exist. That is why it is awesome.

values.value: Five blocks, two page types, a block grid, five images and three published pages. All of it created by an agent through the Umbraco MCP server.
